Definition
The phase lock loop circuit is a very versatile and interesting electronic circuit. Reference Phase Low Pass Comparator Filter Voltage Controlled Oscillator
INTRODUCTIONM
This circuitry has opened up a new world in consumer electronics and communications equipment.
Phase lock loop systems can be configured as frequency multipliers and dividers, FM demodulators and bandpass filters.
It is important that you learn how the circuits operate as you will encounter them many times in your electronics career.

LESSON MENU
PHASE LOCK LOOPSTLE
Most phase lock loop (PLL) circuits are complex and constructed of many components. Integrating the circuit saves a lot of space and simplifies troubleshooting.
DISCUSSION
Since most PLL circuits are in chips, a block diagram and pin out description is all that is needed for circuit analysis.
The basic function of a phase lock loop circuit is to compare the phase and frequency of an oscillator signal with the phase and frequency of an input signal.
The principle component of the circuit is the phase comparator which uses two inputs; one is from a VCO (voltage controlled oscillator) and one is a reference signal.
An output is produced by the phase comparator based on the phase or frequency of the two inputs. The comparator output is a square wave and is called the comparison signal.

The comparison signal is filtered by a low pass filter which creates a smooth DC voltage. The voltage is boosted by an amplifier and sent to the VCO.

The output signal from the VCO can be a sine wave, sawtooth or square wave. The signal from the VCO to the comparator, the comparator to the low pass filter, low pass filter to amplifier, and amplifier to VCO form a closed loop.
Because the circuit is a closed loop, you can begin signal tracing anywhere within the system.
A closed loop system does not alter the input signal. The reference signal and signal from the VCO combine forming a third signal, the comparison signal.
You should note that feedback is not used. Feedback alters the input signal in oscillators and operational amplifiers.
What is the phase comparator's function?
Ensure that the comparison signal is a smooth DC voltage.
Produce an output signal based on the phase and frequency of the input signals.
The phase comparator does not separate the input signals. It compares the two input signals and produces an output.

Now that we have identified each block's main purpose let's look at the system closer and see how the signals are used.
Since the PLL system is a closed loop we can start with the VCO. The voltage controlled oscillator creates an output signal after receiving a DC voltage input.
The output frequency is controlled by the value of the DC voltage, therefore, a VCO has an output frequency that is proportional to it's input voltage.
The output of the VCO is fed to one input of the phase comparator, where it is compared to a reference signal.
The reference signal is also an input to the phase comparator. It can be sent from another oscillator, FM signal source, or the likes.
If the frequency of the VCO is different from the reference signals frequency, the phase comparator creates an error signal or comparison signal.
The comparison signal is a square wave with negative and/or positive pulses, depending upon whether the VCO frequency is higher or lower than the reference input frequency.
The output from the phase comparator is applied to a low pass filter.
Its function is to convert the comparison signal from the comparator to a smooth DC signal, which allows the VCO to operate smoother.
Without the low pass filter the PLL would operate erratically or not at all because the VCO would receive varying pulses.
The amplitude of the converted DC error signal is directly proportional to the phase difference between the comparator's two input signals.

You should note that if the two signals are not equal in frequency, they can only be in phase for a brief instance. In this manner, the phase detector is capable of detecting differences in frequency.
For example, if the reference input has a frequency of 6 Hz and the VCO frequency is 3 Hz, the signals are only in phase every
The greater the phase/frequency difference between the two input signals, the greater the amplitude of the comparison signal.
When the VCO frequency is lagging the reference frequency, the phase comparator, operating in conjunction with the low pass filter, increases the DC output voltage.
The output voltage is fed to the input of the VCO. When the VCO's input voltage is increased the output frequency is increased, catching up to the reference.

When the VCO frequency is leading the reference frequency, the phase comparator and low pass filter lower the DC output voltage, decreasing the VCO's output frequency which ensures that its phase and frequency match the reference signal's.

Once the input signals match, the comparison signal toggles back and forth very rapidly to maintain an error voltage that will keep the output frequency of the VCO at the same frequency as the reference signal frequency.
There is always a comparison signal correcting the VCO frequency, even when the VCO's free running frequency closely matches the reference frequency's.
The error voltage will be 0 VDC only when the free running frequency of the VCO exactly matches the reference signal frequency.
To increase a lagging VCO frequency the DC voltage from the low pass filter _______
A VCO's output frequency is proportional to the input voltage. If the frequency is lagging it needs to be increased.

PLL's have a wide range of applications in the electronics world.
Because of the PLL's ability to lock onto low level signals, even if the input signals are carrying a great deal of interference, they make good Noise Filters and Small Signal Amplifiers.
Because interference is outside the VCO's frequency range it is disregarded.
Being able to limit the frequency range of the PLL also makes it a handy bandpass filter.
A very common use for PLLs is as an FM demodulator.........
The FM transmitter's carrier frequency is used as the center frequency for the VCO.
The received FM signal is the reference input to the phase comparator.
Because the output of the comparator and filter is the difference between the FM signal and the VCO's frequency the output is the demodulated intelligence.
As you know, after the phase detector has determined that the two input frequencies are out of phase, it sends a comparison signal to the low pass filter.
The filter changes the comparison signal to a low frequency AC signal that represents the original intelligence.
With a constantly changing reference signal, as an FM waveform, the VCO is constantly trying to track it.
This means the comparison signal is constantly increasing and decreasing with the FM signal resulting in the demodulated information.
The PLL's specific frequency range make it good for use as
The PLL's ability to lock onto low level signals with interference make it a good noise filter.
TRY AGAIN!
The PLL's ability to constantly compare the reference and VCO signal make it a good FM demodulator.
TRY AGAIN!
PLLs can also be used for digital data transmission and storage. Frequency shift keying (FSK) modulation is a common form used to represent data.
No matter what type of digital information is used in an FSK, the signals are either high or low.
A PLL readily demodulates this data for use within a digital system.
PLL's can be used to synchronize data......................
For instance, many circuits in a computer system must be synchronized to ensure that operations occur in the proper sequence and at the right time.
Using a PLL data synchronizer, the synch signals can be held very accurately.
Larger PLL systems allow synch pulses and data to be shifted throughout on the same line (serial transmission).
PLL frequency syntheziers have replaced older systems that required many crystal oscillators, like CB radios.
Crystal oscillators are expensive and bulky. The PLL frequency synthesizer is relatively inexpensive and compact.
One IC sized frequency synthesizer can replace many crystal oscillators.
Frequency synthesizers are also very accurate and stable making them highly reliable.

As you can see Phase Lock Loop Systems can take on any number of different forms and can be used in a number of different applications but their operation is essentially the same. ise Filter Small Signal Amplifier Bandpass Filter FM Demodulator

1. PLL systems are made of a phase comparator, low pass filter, amplifier and VCO.
2. The phase comparator compares the phase and frequency of a reference signal and VCO signal to produce an output signal called a comparison signal.
3. The comparison signal is a square wave that reflects the phase and frequency difference between the two inputs to the phase comparator.
4. The low pass filter changes the comparison signal to a smooth DC voltage.
5. This voltage is proportional to the phase difference of the comparator's input signals.
6. The amplifier boosts low DC levels for use by the VCO.
7. The VCO changes the DC level to a sine wave, sawtooth or square wave with a frequency that tries to match or lock onto the reference signal's frequency.

PHASE LOCK LOOPITLE
This experiment demonstrates the operation of three phase lock loop configurations along with the phase detection and error amplification sections.
EXPERIMENT
First, let's examine the circuitry that performs the phase detection and error signal amplification functions.
Phase detection is performed by IC1, an MC4044 which is a phase detector circuit contained within a single integrated circuit chip.
The circuit receives two inputs, one of which is an external AC signal (REF IN), the other is the feedback loop from the VCO (FREQ IN).
The output of the phase detector (pins 2 and 13) are fed directly into the corresponding inputs on the charge pump (pins 11
The chip will compare the two signals. If a phase difference is detected an error voltage is produced.
The error voltage is used to change the output frequency of the VCO to rematch the reference frequency.
IC2 is a 741 op amp, it's associated components make up a two pole low pass filter.
R4 and C2 make up a low pass filter whose output is fed to the inverting input of IC2. C1 is a low pass feedback capacitor.
The two pole filter creates a rather smooth DC level on the input of IC3 which is simply a 741 op amp configured as a variable gain amplifier.

Let's now observe the PLL system configured as a frequency synthesizer.
Begin by examining experiment card PC130-224 and its schematic.
IC5 is an internal reference frequency generator circuit formed from a basic 555 timer. Its function is to generate an on-board AC signal for use within the system.
This allows you to observe PLL operation without the requirement of an external AC function generator. This particular frequency generator circuit has a range from 150 Hz to 250 kHz.
The experiment card also contains two binary counters, IC1 and IC2. IC1 receives the pulses from the 555 timer and IC2 receives the pulses from the VCO.

Both counters are connected to 3 switches which allow binary division of the frequency. IC1 uses the reference pulses as a clock input to count down the binary number entered through switches S1-S3 and produce a terminal count pulse for each "N" clock...
The binary range of divisors that S1-S3 can produce is
0 through 7; S1 = bit 0, S2 = bit 1, S3 = bit 2.
IC2 uses the VCO output signal pulses as a clock input to count down the binary number entered through switches S4-S6 and produces a terminal count pulse for each "M" clock.
The binary range of divisors that S4-S6 can produce is
0 through 7; S4 = bit 0, S5 = bit 1, S6 = bit 2.
U1 also functions to clean up the signals, which allows the phase detector to operate better.
U2 and IC2 function the same as U1 and IC1 except that their inputs are from the voltage controlled oscillator.

Let's now observe the PLL system configured as a frequency synthesizer.
Begin by examining experiment card PC130-224 and its schematic.
IC5 is an internal reference frequency generator circuit formed from a basic 555 timer. Its function is to generate an on-board AC signal for use within the system.
This allows you to observe PLL operation without the requirement of an external AC function generator. This particular frequency generator circuit has a range from 120 kHz to 300 kHz..
The experiment card also contains two binary counters, IC1 and IC2. IC1 receives the pulses from the 555 timer and IC2 receives the pulses from the VCO.

Both counters are connected to 3 switches which allow binary division of the frequency. IC1 uses the reference pulses as a clock input to count down the binary number entered through switches S1-S3 and produce a terminal count pulse for each "N" clock...
The binary range of divisors that S1-S3 can produce is
0 through 7; S1 = bit 0, S2 = bit 1, S3 = bit 2.
IC2 uses the VCO output signal pulses as a clock input to count down the binary number entered through switches S4-S6 and produces a terminal count pulse for each "M" clock.
The binary range of divisors that S4-S6 can produce is
0 through 7; S4 = bit 0, S5 = bit 1, S6 = bit 2.
U1 also functions to clean up the signals, which allows the phase detector to operate better.
U2 and IC2 function the same as U1 and IC1 except that their inputs are from the voltage controlled oscillator.
